name: Calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Vigorous fizzing as carbon dioxide bubbles form
The solid calcite gradually disappears
In an open vessel the total mass decreases as gas escapes

explanation.intuition: Acids react with carbonates to make a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas.
explanation.science: Hydrogen ions from the acid react with carbonate ions: CO₃²⁻ + 2 H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂. The calcium ions stay in solution with the chloride ions.
explanation.technical: Net ionic equation: CaCO₃(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). ΔH° ≈ −15 kJ/mol; the reaction is only mildly exothermic.

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 4 (Stoichiometry of chemical reactions)
Royal Society of Chemistry, Practical Chemistry resources (rsc.org)
simplification: Rate is a gameplay constant; real rates depend on surface area, concentration and temperature.

name: Calcium carbonate with acetic acid (vinegar)
observations: Slower fizzing than with hydrochloric acid
Calcite slowly dissolves

explanation.intuition: Vinegar dissolves limestone and eggshells, releasing carbon dioxide bubbles.
explanation.science: Acetic acid is a weak acid, so fewer H⁺ ions are available at any moment and the reaction is slower than with a strong acid at the same concentration.
explanation.technical: CaCO₃(s) + 2 CH₃COOH(aq) → Ca(CH₃COO)₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). No reliable enthalpy value is stored in this database.

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 14 (Acid–base equilibria)
Royal Society of Chemistry, Practical Chemistry resources (rsc.org)
simplification: Weak-acid slowness is represented by a smaller gameplay rate constant, not a kinetic model.

name: Neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: No visible change without an indicator
The solution warms up
An indicator changes colour at the end point

explanation.intuition: An acid and a base cancel each other out, forming a salt and water.
explanation.science: H⁺ ions from the acid combine with OH⁻ ions from the base to form water. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions that remain dissolved.
explanation.technical: Net ionic equation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH° = −55.8 kJ/mol at 25 °C (textbook calorimetry often gives 56–58 kJ/mol).

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 14 (Acid–base titrations)
Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
simplification: The reaction is treated as instantaneous (very fast in reality).

name: Neutralisation of acetic acid by sodium hydroxide
observations: No visible change without an indicator
At the equivalence point the solution is slightly basic

explanation.intuition: Vinegar can be neutralised by a base, forming a salt and water.
explanation.science: Acetic acid transfers its H⁺ to hydroxide. The product, acetate, is a weak base, so the equivalence point is above pH 7.
explanation.technical: CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). Phenolphthalein, not methyl orange, is the right indicator for this titration.

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 14

name: Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Requires very high temperature (a kiln, not a hot plate)
The solid loses mass as carbon dioxide is driven off

explanation.intuition: Strongly heating limestone breaks it down into quicklime and carbon dioxide.
explanation.science: The reaction absorbs energy (endothermic). It only proceeds significantly when the CO₂ pressure in equilibrium with calcite exceeds the surrounding CO₂ pressure, at roughly 900 °C under 1 atm of CO₂.
explanation.technical: ΔH° = +178.3 kJ/mol. The decomposition is reversible; lime kilns sweep away CO₂ to drive it forward.

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 13 (Equilibrium)
Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
simplification: The game uses a sharp threshold temperature (1170 K); the real reaction rate rises gradually with temperature.

name: Electrolysis of brine (chlor-alkali process)
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Bubbles at both electrodes
The solution becomes basic as sodium hydroxide forms

explanation.intuition: Passing electricity through salty water makes sodium hydroxide, hydrogen and chlorine.
explanation.science: Chloride ions are oxidised to Cl₂ at the anode; water is reduced to H₂ and OH⁻ at the cathode. Na⁺ ions stay in solution, so NaOH accumulates.
explanation.technical: Two electrons per Cl₂ molecule. Industrial cells use a membrane to keep the products apart.

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 17
Euro Chlor, 'The chlor-alkali process' (eurochlor.org)
simplification: Gases are collected automatically into sealed canisters; brine electrolysis is chosen over water electrolysis when enough chloride is present.

name: Electrolysis of water
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Bubbles at both electrodes
About twice as much gas forms at the cathode (hydrogen) as at the anode (oxygen)

explanation.intuition: Electricity can split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases.
explanation.science: At the cathode, water gains electrons and forms H₂; at the anode, water loses electrons and forms O₂. Four electrons are transferred for every two water molecules split.
explanation.technical: Faraday's law: moles of reaction = Q / (4F). The minimum voltage is about 1.23 V (ΔG°/zF); real cells need more because of overpotentials. An electrolyte is needed to carry current.

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 17 (Electrochemistry)
Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
simplification: The electrolyte is assumed present; the amount produced follows Faraday's law exactly, but cell voltage requirements are simplified to 'at least 1.23 V'.

name: Synthesis of hydrogen chloride
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: The gas dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid

explanation.intuition: Hydrogen and chlorine combine to make hydrogen chloride, which dissolves to give hydrochloric acid.
explanation.science: Each H–H and Cl–Cl bond is broken and two H–Cl bonds form. The products are lower in energy, so heat is released.
explanation.technical: ΔH° = −184.6 kJ (−92.3 kJ per mole of HCl). Industrially this is done in a controlled burner.

references: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
simplification: Modelled as a controlled synthesis in a sealed vessel containing water; the real reaction can be violent if uncontrolled.

name: Combustion of carbon
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Glowing solid
Releases a large amount of heat

explanation.intuition: Burning carbon (coal, charcoal) combines it with oxygen and releases energy.
explanation.science: Combustion is a rapid exothermic oxidation. The chemical energy released per mole of carbon is the basis of coal-fired heating in the game.
explanation.technical: ΔH° = −393.5 kJ/mol (standard enthalpy of formation of CO₂). Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide instead.

references: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 5 (Thermochemistry)
simplification: Ignition is represented by a threshold temperature.

name: Oxidation of heated copper
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Copper surface turns black
The solid gains mass

explanation.intuition: Heated copper combines with oxygen from the air and gets heavier.
explanation.science: Copper atoms lose electrons (oxidation) and oxygen gains them (reduction). The mass gained equals the mass of oxygen taken from the air — mass is conserved.
explanation.technical: ΔH° = 2 × (−157.3) kJ. Some copper(I) oxide (Cu₂O) also forms in reality.

references: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
Royal Society of Chemistry, Practical Chemistry resources (rsc.org)

name: Slaking of quicklime
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: The mixture becomes very hot
Lumps crumble into a white powder

explanation.intuition: Adding water to quicklime releases a lot of heat.
explanation.science: Calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide; the products have lower energy than the reactants.
explanation.technical: ΔH° = −65.2 kJ/mol. Excess water dissolves a little Ca(OH)₂, giving limewater.

references: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)

name: Limewater test for carbon dioxide
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Clear limewater turns milky as insoluble calcium carbonate forms

explanation.intuition: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky — a classic test for the gas.
explanation.science: CO₂ reacts with dissolved calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate, which is insoluble and appears as a white precipitate.
explanation.technical: With excess CO₂ the precipitate redissolves as calcium hydrogencarbonate; this is not modelled.

references: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
Royal Society of Chemistry, Practical Chemistry resources (rsc.org)

name: Reduction of iron ore with carbon
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Requires a kiln temperature above about 900 °C
Carbon dioxide is released

explanation.intuition: Heating iron ore with carbon removes the oxygen and leaves iron metal.
explanation.science: Carbon is a reducing agent: it takes oxygen from iron(III) oxide. In real blast furnaces most of the reduction is done by carbon monoxide formed from the coke.
explanation.technical: Overall equation 2 Fe₂O₃ + 3 C → 4 Fe + 3 CO₂, ΔH° = +467.9 kJ (the energy comes from burning extra fuel).

references: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 18 (Representative metals)
simplification: The CO intermediate steps are folded into one overall equation.

name: Combustion of hydrogen
deltaHSource: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
observations: Water forms
Large energy release

explanation.intuition: Hydrogen burns in oxygen to form only water.
explanation.science: The reverse of water electrolysis: the energy put in to split water is released again when hydrogen and oxygen recombine.
explanation.technical: ΔH° = −571.6 kJ per 2 mol H₂O(l). Autoignition near 570 °C.

references: Calculated from standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook values)
simplification: Only a controlled reaction inside sealed apparatus is modelled; mixtures of hydrogen and oxygen are dangerous in reality.

name: Iron with hydrochloric acid
observations: Steady fizzing as hydrogen forms
The solution turns pale green
In a sealed vessel the pressure keeps rising

explanation.intuition: Iron dissolves in hydrochloric acid and gives off hydrogen gas.
explanation.science: Iron is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so iron atoms give electrons to H⁺ ions: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ and 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
explanation.technical: Net ionic equation: Fe(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + H₂(g). Hydrogen is flammable; never seal a vessel in which gas is being produced.

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 17 (Electrochemistry: activity series)
Royal Society of Chemistry, Practical Chemistry resources (rsc.org)
simplification: Rate is a gameplay constant; real rates depend on surface area and concentration.

name: Dissolving rust with hydrochloric acid
observations: The red-brown solid dissolves
The solution turns yellow-brown

explanation.intuition: Acid dissolves rust (iron oxide), which is why acids are used to clean steel.
explanation.science: Iron(III) oxide is a basic oxide: its O²⁻ ions combine with H⁺ to make water, leaving Fe³⁺ ions in solution.
explanation.technical: Fe₂O₃(s) + 6 H⁺(aq) → 2 Fe³⁺(aq) + 3 H₂O(l). Industrial 'pickling' of steel uses this reaction.

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 18 (Representative metals)

name: Copper(II) oxide with hydrochloric acid
observations: The black powder dissolves
The solution turns blue-green

explanation.intuition: Black copper oxide dissolves in acid to make a blue-green salt solution.
explanation.science: CuO is a basic oxide, so it neutralises acid just as a hydroxide would, forming a salt and water.

references: Royal Society of Chemistry, Practical Chemistry resources (rsc.org)

name: Sodium hydroxide absorbing carbon dioxide
observations: Gas pressure in a sealed vessel falls as CO₂ is absorbed

explanation.intuition: A sodium hydroxide solution soaks up carbon dioxide.
explanation.science: CO₂ is an acidic oxide; hydroxide ions neutralise it to carbonate.
explanation.technical: 2 OH⁻(aq) + CO₂(g) → CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). This is how CO₂ scrubbers in submarines and spacecraft work (with LiOH).

references: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (openstax.org), chapter 14
